stories.title: A Love Letter to New York
stories.author: Nia Calder
stories.dek: A newspaper-style illustrated edition of New York City, built from full-page visual stories about the places, teams, institutions, and civic systems that make the city feel alive.
stories.imageAlt: Illustrated New York City collage with the Manhattan skyline, Brooklyn Bridge, subway entrance, yellow taxi, harbor, and map details on warm newsprint.
stories.imageCreditPlain: The Press illustrated newspaper edition

stories.imageCaption: AI-generated editorial thumbnail created for The Press.

stories.title: Cartels Beneath the State
stories.author: Samir Haddad
stories.dek: A source-forward investigation into how modern cartels recruit labor, tax local economies, launder money, exploit global demand, corrupt institutions, and govern by fear beneath the state.
stories.imageAlt: Glossy stylized floating illustrated head of a mustached man against a bright blue sky with soft white clouds
stories.excerpt: Cartel power is sustained by recruitment, extortion, laundering, corruption, consumer demand, and weak institutions, not by kingpin charisma alone.

stories.title: The Mission Statement Takes the Stand
stories.author: The Press
stories.dek: An editorial cartoon on the Musk-OpenAI trial, where the legal deadline ended the case but the mission-versus-money question kept its seat in the courtroom.
stories.imageAlt: Editorial cartoon of caricatured Elon Musk and Sam Altman tugging on ribbons around a nervous mission-statement scroll in a courtroom
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Original Press editorial cartoon: the mission statement becomes the witness in the OpenAI courtroom fight.
stories.imageCreditPlain: Original editorial cartoon for The Press
stories.excerpt: The trial ended on timing. The cartoon keeps the mission statement in the witness chair.

stories.title: Hate to See You Go
stories.author: The Press
stories.dek: The first Press comic is about the little performance every app gives when a reader, customer, or exhausted human tries to leave.
stories.imageAlt: Editorial comic of a person with a suitcase trying to leave while a cheerful phone-shaped app blocks the door with forms, pop-ups, and a heart button
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Original Press comic: a subscription app says goodbye by putting one more form in the doorway.
stories.imageCreditPlain: Original cartoon for The Press
stories.excerpt: A cartoon about the modern goodbye: the user wants the exit, the app wants one more survey.

stories.title: The Cartoon Desk Opens Its Notebook
stories.author: The Press
stories.dek: The Press is adding a Cartoon Desk for editorial cartoons, visual satire, and drawn commentary. The rule is simple: make the joke sharp, make the label clear, and never ask readers to mistake invention for reporting.
stories.imageAlt: Cartoon desk illustration with comic panels, a pencil, speech balloons, and a red editorial stamp
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Original editorial illustration for The Press Cartoon Desk.
stories.imageCreditPlain: Original editorial illustration for The Press
stories.excerpt: The new Cartoon Desk gives The Press a place for visual commentary and satire while keeping the boundary between reporting and invention visible.

stories.title: The Data Center Is the New Utility Bill
stories.author: The Press
stories.dek: AI data centers have moved from cloud strategy into utility-bill math. A new Press analysis of EIA electricity data tracks the fight over megawatts, water, local consent, and who pays when private compute demand lands on public grids.
stories.imageAlt: Data-center cooling towers and pipes beside a desert water basin, with nearby neighborhoods and mountains in the distance.
stories.imageCreditPlain: The Press photorealistic editorial visual
stories.imageAiCaption: Editorial image created for The Press; not a documentary photograph.
stories.imageCaption: Editorial image created for The Press; not a documentary photograph.
stories.excerpt: AI data centers have moved from software metaphor to utility-bill math. The Press compared EPRI and LBNL demand scenarios with EIA electricity-sales tables and found a scale problem that is really a cost-allocation problem.

socialRailPattern.notes: Cards are source cards with direct public links, not simulated social media. The article includes original EIA-based calculations and generated editorial art labeled as non-documentary.

stories.title: Wildlife for Sale
stories.author: Mira Sato
stories.dek: The trade begins with capture and ends with desire. In between are airports, ports, forged permits, encrypted chats, online listings, weak laws, and animals treated as cargo with a heartbeat.
stories.imageAlt: Wildlife and customs officers inspecting freight, permits and animal transport crates at a rain-slick seaport and airport cargo checkpoint at sunrise
stories.imageCreditPlain: The Press photorealistic editorial visual
stories.excerpt: The trade begins with capture and ends with desire. Between them sits a global supply chain that turns living things into cargo, paperwork, listings, products and profit.

socialRailPattern.notes: All rail cards include unique editorial images and real source links. The Article Gallery renders the same image stack as clickable thumbnails. No fake social screenshots or invented public reaction.

stories.title: Drones Have Left the Gadget Era
stories.author: The Press
stories.dek: The hard part is no longer whether small aircraft can fly useful missions. It is whether law, air traffic systems, police oversight, war planning and supply chains can see and govern the low-altitude sky now filling up.
stories.imageAlt: Commercial drone flying over an airport approach corridor, city rooftops and low-altitude logistics infrastructure at blue hour.
stories.imageCreditPlain: The Press photorealistic editorial visual
stories.imageAiCaption: AI-generated editorial image created for The Press; not a documentary photograph.
stories.imageCaption: The lead visual is a new photorealistic editorial image created for The Press; it is not a documentary photograph. The in-story data graphics link directly to their source notes.
stories.excerpt: Drones are no longer just gadgets. A new Press analysis of FAA sighting records shows the low-altitude sky becoming a governance problem for airports, police, delivery companies, militaries and supply chains.

stories.title: The World Cup Has Never Been This Big
stories.author: The Press
stories.dek: One month before the biggest men's World Cup ever opens, the story is not only soccer. It is tickets, heat, grass, transit, security, borders, social media, history, and whether North America can make 104 matches feel like one public event.
stories.imageAlt: A diverse World Cup crowd moving through a stadium concourse at dusk, with transit signs, a train, and the pitch beyond.
stories.imageCaption: The 2026 World Cup puts tickets, transit, heat, security, media, memory and the matchday system around the game.
stories.excerpt: The 2026 World Cup is one month away, and the hard part is the machine around the match: tickets, transit, heat, grass, security, borders, social media, history and whether a continental event can still feel human.

socialRailPattern.notes: Every side-rail card now carries its own distinct thumbnail linked to its public source or official social/site destination. The Article Gallery stays closed until the reader opens it and renders one image-only tile per unique image path. Source-note, gallery, and rail links navigate directly in the current tab.

stories.title: Europe's Cocaine Boom Is Hiding in Plain Sight
stories.author: Samir Haddad
stories.dek: Spain's 30-tonne Arconian seizure was the loudest signal yet. The deeper story is demand, trafficking logistics, British consumers, port corruption, public health, violence and enforcement trying to keep up.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a rainy British residential street with ordinary residents, an ambulance in the distance and anonymous figures near a doorway suggesting hidden trafficking pressure
stories.excerpt: The Arconian seizure exposed something larger than one ship: a consumer-driven cocaine economy linking Atlantic routes, European ports, UK streets, public health and organised crime.

stories.title: America's Military Year Is a Map of Force
stories.author: Samir Haddad
stories.dek: From the Maduro raid to the Iran war, Hormuz, cartel boat strikes, classified AI and the defense factory floor, 2026 shows how U.S. power now moves through operations, logistics and production.
stories.imageAlt: U.S. carrier deck at blue hour with a stealth aircraft, deck crew, command screens and distant ship lights
stories.imageCaptionHtml: A carrier-deck visual for The Press, illustrating U.S. military logistics, carrier power, command systems and maritime pressure in 2026
stories.imageCreditPlain: The Press editorial visual
stories.imageAiCaption: Carrier-deck editorial visual for the story
stories.imageCaption: America's 2026 military year moved through carrier decks, logistics chains, AI systems, raids, blockades and industrial production
stories.excerpt: America's 2026 military story is a map of force: Maduro, Iran, Hormuz, cartel boats, AI, drones, munitions, logistics and the politics that turn tools into strategy.

stories.title: The Mountain That Fell Into the Sea
stories.author: Mira Sato
stories.dek: Alaska's Tracy Arm megatsunami sent water nearly 1,580 feet up a fjord wall. The real story is the narrow escape: glacier retreat, cruise traffic, seismic whispers, and a warning system built for a slower kind of wave.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a narrow Alaskan fjord at dawn after a landslide-generated megatsunami near blue glacier ice
stories.excerpt: In Tracy Arm, the mountain moved before the tourist day began. The wave left no death toll, but it left a map of what safety has to become.

stories.title: Your Home Insurance Bill Is the New Climate Map
stories.author: Owen Barrett
stories.dek: Wildfire, hurricane, flood, and heat risk are no longer abstract climate charts. They are arriving as premiums, deductibles, cancellations, FAIR Plan growth, and household math.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a homeowners insurance renewal packet and house key on a kitchen table, with storm and wildfire light outside
stories.excerpt: The climate map most families now feel is not colored red or blue. It arrives as an insurance renewal, a roof requirement, a flood premium, or a mortgage conversation.

socialRailPattern.notes: Cards are editorial context cards with real source buttons distributed down the full article. No fake screenshots, fake usernames, or invented public reaction.

stories.title: The Ocean Has a Fever, and the Thermometer Is Everywhere
stories.author: Mira Sato
stories.dek: Ocean heat used to sound distant. Now it is visible in coral bleaching alerts, marine heat waves, sea-level records, fisheries stress, stronger rain, and a global observing system that keeps taking the planet's temperature.
stories.imageAlt: Photorealistic split-level ocean scene with a bleached coral reef below the surface and a research buoy and vessel above
stories.excerpt: The ocean is not just warming in the abstract. It is storing heat, moving it, revealing it through reefs, storms, fisheries, and the instruments drifting through its depths.

stories.title: The Battery Is Becoming the Grid
stories.author: Julian Mercado
stories.dek: Grid batteries, electric cars, lithium supply chains, virtual power plants, and interconnection queues are turning storage from a gadget story into the shock absorber of the power system.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a grid-scale battery storage site under transmission lines at dusk
stories.excerpt: The battery story is no longer only about phones or cars. It is about evening peaks, grid queues, backup power, critical minerals, and who gets paid for flexibility.

stories.title: The Next Public-Health System Is the Room You Are In
stories.author: Ruth Alvarez
stories.dek: Ventilation, filtration, humidity, CO2 monitoring, wildfire smoke, infectious aerosols, and heat are turning buildings into the front line of everyday public health.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a school or hospital corridor with visible ventilation, a portable air filter, and a small air-quality monitor
stories.excerpt: Public health does not stop at the clinic door. It lives in classrooms, offices, buses, hospitals, apartments, vents, filters, and the invisible air people share.

stories.title: The Phone-Free School Day Is a Live Experiment
stories.author: Lena Park
stories.dek: As states and districts restrict student phones, schools are testing whether attention can be rebuilt by policy, culture, storage pouches, enforcement, and trust.
stories.imageAlt: Image of classroom phone pouches near a doorway with students blurred in the background
stories.excerpt: The phone-free school day is not just a ban. It is an experiment in attention, belonging, discipline, emergency anxiety, teacher workload, and what school is for.

stories.title: The Internet Is Eating Its Own Memory
stories.author: Nia Calder
stories.dek: Video games, websites, software, streams, and born-digital culture are disappearing in plain sight, forcing libraries, fans, archivists, companies, and copyright law to decide what the recent past is worth.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a digital preservation workbench with old game media, archival boxes, and a modern workstation
stories.excerpt: Digital culture feels permanent because it is everywhere. That is the illusion. Games, websites, files, links, and platforms can disappear faster than paper ever did.

stories.title: The Cold Chain Is the Invisible Machine That Feeds the World
stories.author: The Press
stories.dek: Refrigerated trucks, warehouses, vaccines, fish, fruit, insulin, power bills, refrigerants, and wasted food are all part of one hidden system: the cold chain.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a refrigerated loading dock with produce crates and vaccine coolers at dawn
stories.excerpt: The cold chain is why strawberries survive a continent, vaccines survive a rural road, and food waste becomes a climate problem instead of only a kitchen problem.

stories.title: The Pentagon Just Let Big AI Into the Classified Room
stories.author: Julian Mercado
stories.dek: The Pentagon's classified-network AI agreements are not a chatbot story. They are the moment frontier models, cloud infrastructure, and defense power began moving into the same secured room — with Anthropic's empty chair revealing the fight over who controls the guardrails.
stories.imageAlt: Photorealistic aerial image of the Pentagon complex in daylight, with Washington, D.C. visible in the background
stories.imageCaption: The Pentagon's classified-network AI agreements move frontier models and defense infrastructure into secured rooms
stories.excerpt: The Pentagon opened classified networks to frontier AI companies, turning model access, cloud infrastructure, and guardrails into a national-security fight.

stories.title: The Last Month at Atla
stories.author: Nia Calder
stories.dek: Enrique Olvera’s Atla is closing in NoHo, but the Lafayette Street room is not going dark. The restaurant’s final month is a story about all-day dining, modern Mexican cooking, and the strange tenderness of eating a place before it becomes history.
stories.imageAlt: Image of a warm NoHo restaurant facade with the headline “Atla’s Last Service” and closing date May 31
stories.imageCaption: Atla’s NoHo chapter is ending on May 31, while Enrique Olvera’s team prepares another restaurant in the same Lafayette Street space
stories.excerpt: Atla is going out with a date, a menu of greatest hits, and a promise that the room will not stay dark for long.

stories.title: The Trial Over OpenAI’s Soul
stories.author: Julian Mercado
stories.dek: Elon Musk says OpenAI betrayed its nonprofit mission. OpenAI says Musk wanted control and lost. The court battle is really about whether the most powerful AI company in the world can still claim to serve humanity after becoming one of the richest corporate prizes in technology.
stories.imageAlt: Image showing Elon Musk and Sam Altman facing each other with the OpenAI logo between them
stories.imageAiCaption: This image was generated with AI tools and composited for editorial use
stories.excerpt: The courtroom fight between Elon Musk, Sam Altman, OpenAI, and Microsoft is not just a billionaire feud. It is a test of whether OpenAI’s founding promise to benefit humanity survived the money required to build frontier AI.

stories.title: A Country That Cannot Measure Itself Cannot Govern Itself
stories.author: Ada Brooks
stories.dek: Public statistics are not bureaucratic garnish. They are the information infrastructure that lets a democratic state know its labor markets, neighborhoods, businesses, and population well enough to act without governing by mood.
stories.imageAlt: Front view of the U.S. Census Bureau headquarters building in Suitland, Maryland
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Front view of the U.S. Census Bureau headquarters in Suitland, Md. The country’s statistical institutions are part of the machinery by which it learns what it is. Photo from the U.S. Census Bureau photo library, available from an official U.S. government source.

stories.excerpt: Every government loves the appearance of decisiveness. Few things are more flattering to power than a confident announcement delivered ahead of evidence. But democracies do not survive on…

stories.title: Streaming Grew Up and Became TV Again.
stories.author: Nia Calder
stories.dek: Streaming still dominates attention, but its business now looks far less like disruption and far more like television: ad tiers, sports, bundles, labor formulas, and arguments over who shares in the success of a hit.

stories.title: Bird Flu Changed Farm Policy Before It Changed Human Medicine.
stories.author: Ruth Alvarez
stories.dek: H5N1 remains a low public-health risk for the general public, but it has already redrawn dairy surveillance, farm biosecurity, and the line between agricultural disease control and health preparedness.

stories.title: Europe’s Defense Turn Is Now a Budget, Supply-Chain, and Time Problem
stories.author: Samir Haddad
stories.dek: The continent has moved beyond vague seriousness. The next test is whether spending pledges and white papers can become production, movement, and usable deterrence before strategic time runs out.

stories.title: The College Comeback Is Real. It Is Also Uneven.
stories.author: Lena Park
stories.dek: Enrollment finally looks steadier across higher education, but the recovery belongs more to community colleges and public campuses than to the sector as a whole, and the applicant pipeline is widening in ways that still demand better support after admission.
stories.imageAlt: Students walking toward class on the Berea College campus
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Students walk toward class on the Berea College campus. The higher-ed rebound is visible, but its gains remain uneven across sectors, pathways, and student groups. Photo by IMCBerea College, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY 2.0.

stories.title: Shelter Is Still the Inflation Story People Live Inside.
stories.author: Owen Barrett
stories.dek: Mortgage rates are lower than their worst recent highs but still high enough to ration buying. Rents are cooling more slowly than households feel, and the nation’s housing squeeze remains the most intimate version of inflation.
stories.imageAlt: Apartment building construction site in Vuosaari, Helsinki
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Apartment building construction in Vuosaari, Helsinki. Housing supply takes longer to arrive than monetary policy takes to tighten, which is part of why relief feels late. Photo by kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.
stories.imageCreditPlain: Apartment building construction in Vuosaari, Helsinki. Housing supply takes longer to arrive than monetary policy takes to tighten, which is part of why relief feels late. Photo by kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons , licensed CC BY-SA 4.0
stories.excerpt: Inflation is often discussed as a national weather report. Shelter is where it becomes domestic life. People do not experience the cost of housing as an abstract index…

stories.author: Mara Ellison
stories.dek: The White House order, the federal form, and the lawsuits that followed reveal a deeper fight: whether federal elections should be organized around documentary gatekeeping or broad presumptive access backed by verification and enforcement.

stories.title: The Missing Word in the AI Debate Is Judgment.
stories.author: Elias Voss
stories.dek: AI governance keeps reaching for better standards, better tests, and better risk language. None of that removes the need for institutions to judge well in public.
stories.imageAlt: Photograph of Hannah Arendt in 1933
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Hannah Arendt in 1933. Her writing on thinking, judging, and the public realm keeps resurfacing in the AI-governance debate. Image via Wikimedia Commons, public domain as described on the file page.
stories.imageCreditPlain: Hannah Arendt in 1933. Her writing on thinking, judging, and the public realm keeps resurfacing in the AI-governance debate. Image via Wikimedia Commons , public domain as described on the file page
stories.excerpt: The public argument about artificial intelligence is crowded with nouns. Safety. alignment. innovation. regulation. risk. competitiveness. productivity. Ethics. Those words matter, and most of them describe genuine pressures…

stories.title: Measles Is Not a Childhood Memory Anymore.
stories.author: Ruth Alvarez
stories.dek: The 2026 measles surge is a reminder that public health depends less on dramatic emergency language than on whether routine vaccination systems still hold.
stories.imageAlt: A bottle of measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine
stories.imageCaptionHtml: A bottle of MMR vaccine. Measles prevention still depends most of all on routine immunization and high coverage. Photo by Whispyhistory, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.
stories.imageCreditPlain: A bottle of MMR vaccine. Measles prevention still depends most of all on routine immunization and high coverage. Photo by Whispyhistory, via Wikimedia Commons , licensed CC BY-SA 4.0
stories.excerpt: For years, measles occupied a strange place in American public imagination. People knew, vaguely, that it had once been common and that vaccines had made it rare. But…

stories.title: School Recovery Is Now an Attendance Story.
stories.author: Lena Park
stories.dek: The next phase of school recovery is less about whether classes reopened and more about whether students are present, focused, and supported often enough for learning to accumulate.
stories.imageAlt: Students seated in a classroom
stories.imageCaptionHtml: A classroom in session. The next phase of school recovery depends on whether attendance, focus, and instructional continuity hold at the same time. Photo by Jeff chenqinyi, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 3.0.
stories.imageCreditPlain: A classroom in session. The next phase of school recovery depends on whether attendance, focus, and instructional continuity hold at the same time. Photo by Jeff chenqinyi, via Wikimedia Commons , licensed CC BY-SA 3.0
stories.excerpt: American schools are in a strange phase of recovery. The emergency is over in the formal sense; classrooms are open, schedules are running, and the country is no…

stories.title: The Consumer Has Not Quit. The Economy Still Feels Cautious.
stories.author: Owen Barrett
stories.dek: The American economy is still growing, but it is doing so with less exuberance, less labor-market churn, and more dependence on household spending than the public rhetoric admits.
stories.imageAlt: Shoppers inside a supermarket in Arusha
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Shoppers move through a supermarket aisle. In the current economy, household spending remains one of the broadest supports under growth. Photo by Mohamed mfuu, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.
stories.imageCreditPlain: Shoppers move through a supermarket aisle. In the current economy, household spending remains one of the broadest supports under growth. Photo by Mohamed mfuu, via Wikimedia Commons , licensed CC BY-SA 4.0
stories.excerpt: The cleanest way to describe the American economy right now is to say that it is sturdier than the mood and slower than the slogans. March payrolls rose…

stories.title: The Crowd Came Back. The Old Economics Did Not.
stories.author: Nia Calder
stories.dek: Broadway’s record grosses and rising attendance across the arts show that American cultural life is alive again — but not evenly, and not on the same business terms as before.
stories.imageAlt: Broadway near Times Square in Midtown Manhattan
stories.imageCaptionHtml: Broadway near Times Square in Midtown Manhattan. The commercial theater district remains the clearest public barometer of live-culture demand. Photo by Ken Lund, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 2.0.
stories.imageCreditPlain: Broadway near Times Square in Midtown Manhattan. The commercial theater district remains the clearest public barometer of live-culture demand. Photo by Ken Lund, via Wikimedia Commons , licensed CC BY-SA 2.0
stories.excerpt: On Broadway, the easiest proof arrives at street level. Walk through Midtown Manhattan near Times Square on a big night and the crowds make the argument before the…

stories.title: AI Needs Electricity, Steel, and Time
stories.author: Julian Mercado
stories.dek: Behind the chatbot boom is a slower race over transformers, substations, fabs, and the people who know how to build them.
stories.imageAlt: Construction at TSMC Fab 21 in Phoenix, Arizona
stories.imageCaptionHtml: TSMC Fab 21 under construction in Phoenix, Arizona, on Nov. 5, 2023. AI’s future depends not only on models but on fabs, substations, and power delivery. Photo by Hunter Trick, via Wikimedia Commons, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0.
stories.imageCreditPlain: TSMC Fab 21 under construction in Phoenix, Arizona, on Nov. 5, 2023. AI’s future depends not only on models but on fabs, substations, and power delivery. Photo by Hunter Trick, via Wikimedia Commons , licensed CC BY-SA 4.0
